title: Microtask Batcher (Coalesce Multiple Calls into Single Turn)
concept: Event Loop Turn Coalescing & Batch Updating
problemStatement: Build `createBatcher(flushCallback)` that batches multiple synchronous updates and triggers `flushCallback(accumulatedItems)` exactly ONCE in the microtask queue at the end of the current synchronous turn.
interviewTrap: Calling the flush callback for every item or using `setTimeout` (which introduces a 4ms minimum delay and runs after UI rendering).

testCases.name: Batches multiple synchronous calls into one flush
testCases.testFn: const flushes = []; const batcher = createBatcher(items => flushes.push(items)); batcher(1); batcher(2); batcher(3); await Promise.resolve(); return flushes;

testCases.name: Subsequent turns trigger new independent batches
testCases.input: batch in turn 1 and batch in turn 2
testCases.testFn: const flushes = []; const batcher = createBatcher(items => flushes.push(items)); batcher(10); await Promise.resolve(); batcher(20); await Promise.resolve(); return flushes;

testCases.name: Flush receives full item set in exact insertion order
testCases.testFn: let res = null; const batcher = createBatcher(items => { res = items; }); batcher('a'); batcher('b'); batcher('c'); await Promise.resolve(); return res;

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A Microtask Batcher coalesces multiple synchronous calls made during the same event loop turn into a single batched flush executed in the subsequent microtask checkpoint, preventing redundant calculations or layout thrashing.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Maintain an internal array `items = []` and a boolean `scheduled = false`.
If `!scheduled`, set `scheduled = true` and schedule a flush via `queueMicrotask(flush)`.
In `flush()`, reset `scheduled = false`, snapshot `const batch = items.slice()`, clear `items = []`, and call `flushCallback(batch)`.
Subsequent calls in the next turn initiate a fresh independent batch.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: This is the exact mechanism React and Vue use for batching DOM updates and state setters. By leveraging `queueMicrotask` or `Promise.resolve()`, 100 synchronous state updates within one event turn collapse into exactly 1 re-render job.

complexity.time: O(1) per add operation; O(K) where K is batch size on flush.
complexity.space: O(K) temporary queue space in memory.

edgeCasesHandled: Multiple synchronous calls in the same turn execute only 1 flush.
Items are preserved in exact insertion order.
New items added in subsequent turns trigger a new batch cleanly.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Why is microtask batching superior to macrotask (setTimeout) batching for UI frameworks?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Microtasks execute before the browser paints the next screen frame. If you batch DOM updates using `queueMicrotask`, the browser reconciles all updates in a single paint cycle without visual flashing (FOUC). If you used `setTimeout(0)`, the browser might paint intermediate states across multiple frames, causing noticeable UI flickering and layout thrashing.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests understanding of how event loop queues integrate with browser rendering engines.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How does a microtask batcher ensure thread safety in a single-threaded language?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Because JavaScript is single-threaded and non-preemptive (run-to-completion), synchronous calls to `.add()` populate an in-memory queue without interleaving. The boolean flag `isScheduled` is checked and set synchronously, guaranteeing that exactly one microtask flush is enqueued for that turn.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Validates grasp of single-threaded run-to-completion invariants.

realWorldUseCases.description: Vue batches component re-renders triggered by reactive property mutations into a microtask queue, flushing all watchers once per event loop turn.
realWorldUseCases.codeSnippet: function queueWatcher(watcher) { queue.push(watcher); if (!waiting) { waiting = true; nextTick(flushQueue); } }

realWorldUseCases.description: GraphQL DataLoader collects individual item IDs requested during the synchronous resolver tree execution and fires a single `SELECT * WHERE id IN (...)` SQL query on the microtask tick.
realWorldUseCases.codeSnippet: loader.load(1); loader.load(2); // coalesced into single SQL batch

howToExplain.opening: A microtask batcher aggregates multiple synchronous operations occurring within the same tick into a single coordinated execution, eliminating redundant recalculations.
keyPoints: A synchronous boolean flag guarantees only one flush job is scheduled per tick.
Items accumulate in an array during synchronous code execution.
The microtask runs immediately after the synchronous turn before rendering occurs.
This pattern is the foundation of modern state batching in React, Vue, and GraphQL.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Coalescing synchronous operations into microtasks is the primary design pattern for achieving high performance in UI frameworks and data loaders.
analogies: Like an office mail room: instead of running to the post office for every single letter dropped in the outgoing tray, you collect letters all morning and make a single trip at noon.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to reset the scheduled flag inside the flush handler.
commonMistakes.why: If the flag is not reset, future calls to add() in subsequent turns will never schedule a flush, dropping future batches.
commonMistakes.correct: Always reset `isScheduled = false` at the very beginning of the flush function.

followUpDeepDive.question: How did React 18 change batching semantics compared to React 17?
followUpDeepDive.answer: In React 17, batching was limited to React event handlers. Updates inside `setTimeout`, `fetch`, or native events were not batched and triggered multiple renders. In React 18, 'Automatic Batching' uses internal microtask and lane scheduling to batch ALL updates, regardless of where they originate.
